text: The last lesson left a gap: when a spot worker node gets reclaimed, does the whole job have to stop and restart just because the node count changed? Not necessarily. Elastic training lets a job's membership shrink and grow at runtime, within limits, instead of treating every change as a full restart.

Instead of a fixed node count, an elastic launch specifies a range — here, one to sixty-four nodes. Max restarts caps how many times the elastic agent will try reforming the group before giving up for real. And the c10d rendezvous backend is what makes reforming possible at all — surviving ranks re-discover each other and agree on a new membership without a human re-launching anything.

When a worker disappears, surviving ranks detect it through a timeout on the next collective call, tear down the current process group, and re-enter rendezvous together. Once they agree on a new, smaller world size, training resumes — from the last checkpoint, not from scratch, since in-memory state on the survivors was built for the old world size.

It's worth being precise here: the in-flight step that was running when the worker disappeared is lost — there's no resuming a half-finished collective. What elastic training avoids is the job being marked failed and sitting there until a human notices and resubmits it. And it isn't unlimited — a flapping node eventually exhausts the restart budget, and the node-count floor is set well above one, because training on a handful of nodes is often not worth continuing versus waiting for replacement capacity.

Elastic training turns what would be a failed job needing manual resubmission into a short, self-healing pause. Next up, lesson twenty-three: designing for node failure, pulling the whole chapter together.
